slides.title: VR Forge — Help
slides.html:
VR Forge asks a model or a local CLI agent to build a complete, multi-file WebXR project for the Meta Quest 3 — a game, a simulation, or a tool — and then does the thing that makes it worth having: it runs the project in an immersive session and measures what happened.

That is the whole point. "It works in VR" is otherwise the least verifiable claim in this hub: the artefact runs on a device the browser cannot see, in a session that cannot start without a user gesture, at a frame rate no desktop reproduces. VR Forge converts the biggest part of that — did it actually enter VR and render two eyes? — from a claim into a measurement, and is explicit about the part it cannot answer.

slides.title: The app
slides.html: This is the app as it opens. Every screenshot in this deck is captured from the running app, not drawn by hand.

slides.title: Setup
slides.html:
1. Pick a provider/model, or a CLI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) from the executor dropdown. The gear opens provider settings.

  2. Connect a data root (folder icon). Every build is written to disk under <root>/vr-forge/projects/<brief>/<runId>/ — nothing is ever overwritten. New run folders begin with the local start date and time (YYYY-MM-DD_HH-mm-ss), keep their unique run ID, and end with a short model name (or the CLI agent plus default when no model was selected). Existing folders still open normally.

  3. Optional but recommended: run the hub with python3 serve.py 8084. That adds the CLI-agent bridge and the Quest bridge (headset status, one-click open on the headset). Without it, everything else still works.

  4. For the headset itself there are two routes, and you can use either:

    • Over Wi-Fi (no cable, no adb). Start the hub with python3 serve.py 8084 --host 0.0.0.0 --https-port 8443 and open the https://…:8443/ link it prints in Quest Browser. Accept the certificate warning once (Advanced → Proceed). You can then use VR Forge on the headset: build a brief and open the result in VR from the same browser.
    • adb reverse. Follow prompt-gallery/QUEST-VR-ACCESS.md: developer mode, adb over Wi-Fi, and adb reverse tcp:8084 tcp:8084. The Quest then reaches this hub at http://localhost:8084/, which Quest Browser treats as a trusted origin — so WebXR works without HTTPS.

    Why two: a browser only offers Enter VR on a secure address. localhost counts and so does HTTPS; plain http://192.168.x.x does not, so over that address a project opens flat (its desktop fallback) and never enters VR.

slides.title: Briefs
slides.html:
The Library holds 31 seed briefs across three kinds — games, simulations and apps — including one deliberate control cell (Raw WebXR, No Libraries) and one passthrough/mixed-reality brief.

Sixteen of them are large simulations, grouped by subcategory: economics (macroeconomy sandbox, order-book floor), urban planning (planning table, transit network lab), logistics (single-SKU pallets, mixed-SKU 3D packing, cylindrical loads, warehouse pick-paths), traffic (junction lab, evacuation and crowd flow), defence (command sand table, sustainment planner) and the universe (atlas of scale, N-body cluster, curved spacetime, galaxy formation). Each one names the actual model it must implement — IDM and MOBIL, social forces, extreme-point packing, Barnes-Hut, Schwarzschild geodesics — and its acceptance list is written so a reviewer can check the model, not the graphics.

Your own briefs live beside them in the data root and are versioned; seeds can be hidden but never lose their history.

slides.title: Briefs (cont.)
slides.html:
A VR brief says more than a sentence of prose, because the checks that follow have to be checkable:

Field What it decides
kind game / simulation / app — the taxonomy and the coach's framing
xrMode immersive-vr, immersive-ar (passthrough), or both
interaction controllers, hands, locomotion, haptics
xrFeatures the WebXR features the session may require or request
comfort target fps, vignette on motion, snap turn, seated support
desktopFallback required: how the project is reviewed without a headset
scene what must actually be in the scene
acceptance the statements a reviewer checks it against
hubServices opt-in runtime access to the hub: ask, image, agent

desktopFallback is required, not optional. A VR project with no review path outside a headset cannot be looked at, diffed, screenshotted or compared — and the validator needs it too.

slides.title: Hub services — a simulation that can ask
slides.html:
A generated project is served by the hub, and on the Quest it reaches the hub through the adb reverse. So a brief can opt into three things a static page cannot do for itself, through the provisioned lib/hub-bridge.js:

Call What it does Needs
HubBridge.ask({ prompt }) one model answer — an in-sim economist, an intel summary, a planning review OPENROUTER_API_KEY or HUB_ASK_BASE_URL in serve.py's environment, or a local OpenAI-compatible server on 127.0.0.1:1234
HubBridge.askJson({ prompt }) the same, parsed — a generated scenario, policy weights, dialogue as above
HubBridge.image({ prompt }) a generated texture as a data URL a reachable Wan2GP node
HubBridge.agent({ prompt }) a local CLI coding agent for heavier work the agent bridge (no API key: it uses your CLI login)

Four rules hold this together, and the validator or the system prompt enforces each one:

slides.title: Hub services — a simulation that can ask (cont.)
slides.html:
1. The project never sees a key. Whatever provider is configured lives in the server's environment. /__ask resolves it, caps the prompt and token count, and rate-limits (20 calls a minute, 500 a run, all tunable).
  2. The simulation must work without any of it. Hub-backed features are enrichment on a scene that already runs: procedural textures when no image comes back, built-in scenario data when no model answers, a visible "unavailable" line rather than a dead control. HubBridge.status() says what is actually available; the brief's acceptance list should require the degraded path.
  3. Never call from the animation loop. A model call takes seconds and the hub rate-limits — a per-frame call stalls the headset and burns the budget. Ask on a deliberate action and show the previous answer meanwhile.
  4. A project that calls the hub is not portable, and says so. The run is marked hub-bound with the endpoints it used; exported on its own it keeps the simulation and loses those features. A project that calls a hub endpoint its brief never asked for fails validation.

slides.title: Hub services — a simulation that can ask (cont.)
slides.html:
Turn it on for your own briefs with hubServices: { ask: 'optional' } and the hub-bridge library. Nine seed briefs already use it.

Configure the model service before starting the hub, for example:

OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... python3 serve.py 8084
# or any OpenAI-compatible server, local or remote:
HUB_ASK_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1 HUB_ASK_MODEL=my-model python3 serve.py 8084

GET /__ask/status reports what is configured — and never the key.

slides.title: The XR contract
slides.html:
Five rules are in the system prompt and enforced by the validator, so the app never fails a build for a requirement it did not state:

  1. The session entry control carries data-forge-id="enter-xr", and forge-project.json names it in xr.entryControl. Nothing outside the project can start an immersive session; without this the build cannot be verified at all.
  2. The project renders without a session. No navigator.xr, or an unsupported mode, must produce the declared desktop fallback and a visible explanation — never an exception, never a blank page.
  3. Everything is project-local. No CDN, no https:// reference. The headset reaches the project through a loopback tunnel with no internet. The one exception is the hub's own same-origin endpoints, and only for a brief that asked for hub services (above).
  4. What it requests is what it declared. The mode and features passed to requestSession must match the manifest.
  5. An import map maps only to project-local files.

slides.title: Build
slides.html: The Build view is the trace on the left and three ways to look at one project on the right.

slides.title: Build (cont.)
slides.html:
• Desktop — the project's non-XR path in a blob-URL iframe, live as files land. This is the fallback, not the product.

  • XR session — an emulated Quest 3. Start the emulator, press Enter XR, and the project's own entry control is clicked. Live readouts show frames presented, per-frame callback cost and the number of eye views; the controls press the emulated trigger, push the thumbstick, recentre the headset, and switch the primary input between controllers and hands. This is the same harness the validator drives, so what you poke at is what the report measures.

  • On the Quest — the two ways to put this run on the headset. Nothing is copied to the Quest either way: it opens the run straight from the data root.

    • Over Wi-Fi shows the run's address on the hub's network address. When VR Forge is open in the headset's own browser you get Open here, and the pane says plainly whether that browser can enter VR on this address. If it cannot, Open in VR (HTTPS) moves to the hub's HTTPS port (when the hub was started with --https-port); the note underneath also gives the one-time Quest Browser setting that makes the plain address trusted (chrome://flags → Insecure origins treated as secure). On the hub machine the same block gives you the address to open on the headset.
    • adb reverse is headset status from the bridge, the exact http://localhost:8084/_data/… URL, Open on Quest, and Restore reverse for when the headset has slept.

    Older runs have the same pane: in Runs, pick a brief, select one run and press On the Quest.

slides.title: Build (cont.)
slides.html: Pause / Resume and Hard stop work as they do in Game Forge V2: pause parks an in-app build at a safe boundary, or suspends a CLI agent's process, and resume carries on from exactly there.

slides.title: What a run proves — and what it does not
slides.html:
Validation runs in four lanes.

A — Structure. Manifest present and valid, entry exists, every reference resolves, nothing external, provisioned libraries byte-identical to their pins, and the xr block well-formed with an entry control.

B — Desktop. The project boots in a diagnostic frame. Console errors, uncaught exceptions, rejected promises and failed resource loads are errors. A project that throws before its fallback appears fails here whatever it would do in VR.

C — Emulated XR session. The project is loaded again with an emulated Quest 3 (Meta's IWER) installed over navigator.xr and a probe wrapped around the WebXR entry points. Then:

slides.title: What a run proves — and what it does not (cont.)
slides.html:
Check Verdict if it fails
An immersive session was granted error
≥120 frames through XRSession.requestAnimationFrame error
The viewer pose had two views, with different transforms error
The project set one viewport per eye error
The eye framebuffer is not one flat colour error
Requested mode/features match the manifest error
Controllers, select events, haptics the brief asked for warning
95th-percentile frame callback within budget warning
The session ended cleanly warning

The viewport check is the one that catches the classic bug. The runtime hands every project two views, so a project that renders the scene once and lets both eyes see it still gets a healthy-looking pose — but it sets a single full-framebuffer viewport, and that is measurable. (A renderer using OVR_multiview looks the same; say so in the README if that is deliberate.)

slides.title: What a run proves — and what it does not (cont.)
slides.html:
The left eye is read back out of the framebuffer and saved as the run's evidence image — preview.png for a VR run is what the headset would have shown, not a screenshot of a web page.

D — Device. Whether the run was opened on the real headset, and when. This is provenance, never evidence: the hub cannot see what happened after Quest Browser loaded the page.

Honesty limits

slides.title: What a run proves — and what it does not (cont.)
slides.html:
• The emulator is not a Quest. It proves a project enters an immersive session and renders stereo frames. It proves nothing about device performance, thermals, comfort, tracking quality, or how the scale feels.
  • Emulated frame rate is this browser's rAF rate. Frame cost — time inside the project's own callback — is measured and meaningful; frame rate is not, and is never reported as fps achieved on device.
  • Passthrough (immersive-ar) renders a synthetic environment. Plane detection and hit test return the emulator's synthetic geometry, so a room-planner brief is verified as plumbing that works, not as a room that was understood.
  • A run that only passed the emulated lane says emulator-verified, not verified on Quest 3. Put it on the headset before you believe it.

slides.title: Project libraries and lanes
slides.html:
Generated projects never load anything from this repository. Selected libraries are copied into the project's own lib/, checked against pinned hashes before and after generation, and included in the export.

  • three-xr — Three.js 0.185.1 (ES modules) with the WebXR add-ons: VRButton, ARButton, XRButton, XRControllerModelFactory, XRHandModelFactory, XRPlanes, XREstimatedLight, plus GLTFLoader and the geometry/skeleton utilities they need. The briefing hands the model the exact import map. OrbitControls and the post-processing stack are not installed — a few lines of your own beat a 404 in the headset.
  • rapier3d — WASM rigid-body physics, for grabbing, throwing and stacking.
  • tone / howler — synthesis and sound effects.
  • No library — raw WebXR against WebGL2. The control cell.

Lanes pin a brief to a library set so the same brief can be built several ways and compared cell by cell in the Matrix.

slides.title: Runs, Matrix, Batch
slides.html: Every attempt is an append-only run: prompt snapshot, trace, manifest, capability audit, validation report, XR report and eye capture, all on disk. Runs compares them, Matrix lays out (brief × lane), and Batch runs a model or a CLI agent across many briefs. Iteration — fork, improve, repair, continue, merge — always copies into a new run; a heal that makes things worse costs nothing.

slides.title: Project manifest
slides.html:
{
  "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "vr", "entry": "index.html", "runtime": "webxr",
  "xr": {
    "modes": ["immersive-vr"],
    "requiredFeatures": ["local-floor"], "optionalFeatures": ["hand-tracking"],
    "inputs": { "controllers": true, "hands": false, "haptics": true },
    "locomotion": "teleport", "targetFps": 72,
    "entryControl": "[data-forge-id=\"enter-xr\"]"
  },
  "fallback": { "kind": "desktop", "description": "orbit camera + mouse grab" },
  "assets": [], "declaredControls": ["Trigger: grab", "Thumbstick: teleport"]
}

runtime: "webxr" previews like a module-web project. The runtime name quest-native is reserved for a future APK lane; nothing implements it today.

slides.title: Notes & limits
slides.html:
• The Quest bridge is loopback-only. It will open a URL on the headset only when that URL is served by this very server, under the data root. It runs adb; if adb is missing or the headset is asleep, the pane says so and the buttons stay disabled rather than failing silently.
  • A hub without serve.py has no bridge at all. The Quest pane then shows the URL to open by hand, and the CLI-agent rows disappear from the executor list (as everywhere else in the hub).
  • The emulated session runs in this page's process. A generated project with a runaway loop can make the app sluggish; stop the emulator, or use the desktop pane, while a heavy build is still writing files.
  • immersive-ar briefs need a Quest 3 to mean anything. The emulator will run them, and the checks about declaration, frames and input still apply, but the passthrough imagery is synthetic.
  • Tests. node --test vr-forge/tests/*.test.mjs covers the probe's analysis, the manifest contract, the seed catalogue and the bridge client; node tools/vr-xr-lane-check.mjs drives the real validator, in a real browser, against two fixture projects that differ by one line — one renders a viewport per eye, the other fills the framebuffer once. The lane is only worth anything if it passes the first and fails the second.
